plan.contextChunk: This figure stacks five drawings of the same fixed string. At the top a horizontal line runs between two black endpoint dots, each labeled "Node", with a double-headed dimension arrow above it labeled L. Beneath come four standing-wave patterns on lines of that same length, labeled at the left n = 1, n = 2, n = 3, and n = 4. Each is a dark blue curve with a pale mirror-image curve, the two outlining the envelope the string sweeps, ends pinned and interior crossing points rising from none to three. Two expressions sit to the right of each: 1/2 lambda_1 = L and lambda_1 = 2/1 L, then lambda_2 = L and lambda_2 = 2/2 L, then 3/2 lambda_3 = L and lambda_3 = 2/3 L, then 4/2 lambda_4 = L and lambda_4 = 2/4 L. A general statement closes the lower right, lambda_n = 2/n L for n = 1, 2, 3, and so on. Holding one length fixed while packing in more half-wavelengths shows how the pinned ends restrict which wavelengths fit. The sequence introduces the normal modes of a string fixed at both ends.

interactionPlan.concept: A string fixed at both ends supports only normal modes whose wavelength packs an exact integer number of half-wavelengths into length L, giving lambda_n = 2L/n; higher n means shorter wavelength and more nodes.
elements: four horizontally stacked rows, one per mode n = 1, 2, 3, 4
row 1: single half-wavelength envelope (dark blue curve + pale mirror), two endpoint node dots, label 'n = 1'
row 1 equations: '(1/2) λ₁ = L' and 'λ₁ = 2L' to the right of the wave
row 2: two half-wavelengths envelope, three node dots (2 endpoints + 1 interior), label 'n = 2'
row 2 equations: '(2/2) λ₂ = L' and 'λ₂ = L' to the right of the wave
row 3: three half-wavelengths envelope, four node dots (2 endpoints + 2 interior), label 'n = 3'
row 3 equations: '(3/2) λ₃ = L' and 'λ₃ = (2/3)L' to the right of the wave
row 4: four half-wavelengths envelope, five node dots (2 endpoints + 3 interior), label 'n = 4'
row 4 equations: '(4/2) λ₄ = L' and 'λ₄ = (1/2)L' to the right of the wave
horizontal equilibrium line through each row
left-side mode label 'n = k' for each row
double-headed dimension arrow labeled 'L' spanning the full width of each row
highlight ring or glow around the currently selected row
general formula 'λ_n = (2/n)L,  n = 1, 2, 3, …' at lower right

interactions.label: Highlight mode
interactions.teaches: All four modes remain visible for comparison; highlighting one row enlarges it slightly and draws attention to how each successive mode packs one more half-wavelength into the same L, shrinking the wavelength

interactions.label: Oscillate highlighted mode
interactions.teaches: The highlighted row animates its string sweeping between the two envelope curves while all node dots stay fixed and antinodes swing through maximum amplitude, reinforcing the node/antinode distinction

demo_steps.title: All four modes at a glance
demo_steps.narration: All four standing-wave modes are displayed simultaneously. Notice how each row adds one more loop (half-wavelength) within the same fixed length L, and the wavelength visibly shrinks from row to row.

demo_steps.title: Fundamental mode (n = 1)
demo_steps.narration: The highlighted n = 1 row shows one half-wavelength spanning the full length: (1/2)λ₁ = L, so λ₁ = 2L. Only the two endpoints are nodes.

demo_steps.title: Higher harmonics
demo_steps.narration: Step through n = 2, 3, 4: each row gains one interior node and one additional loop. The equation pair on each row updates to (n/2)λ_n = L, making the integer-fit condition explicit for every mode.

demo_steps.title: Watch a mode oscillate
demo_steps.narration: Press play on the highlighted mode: the string sweeps between its envelope curves. Nodes stay perfectly still while antinodes swing widest — the visual proof that nodes are points of permanent destructive interference.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Because both ends are pinned nodes, only wavelengths satisfying (n/2)λ_n = L are allowed — stacking all four modes side by side makes the shrinking wavelength and growing node count immediately visible.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Four rows stacked vertically, each showing one normal mode. Every row is always visible — the highlight merely enlarges or brightens the selected row (e.g. slight scale-up, brighter stroke, subtle background tint) while the others remain at normal opacity. Each row contains: left label 'n = k', the standing-wave envelope (solid dark-blue curve + pale light-blue mirror forming the sweep region), node dots on the equilibrium line, a dimension arrow labeled L, and to the right the equation pair '(n/2) λ_n = L' and 'λ_n = (2/n)L' rendered in a comfortable serif math font with clear fraction bars and adequate numerator/denominator spacing. The general formula 'λ_n = (2/n)L, n = 1, 2, 3, …' sits at the lower right. Rows are evenly spaced with enough vertical room that the envelopes do not overlap. Color: dark blue (#1a3a6b) for the live curve, pale desaturated blue (#a8c8e8) for the mirror envelope. Node dots are solid black. The highlighted row gets a soft warm background band or a 2px accent border to distinguish it without hiding the others.

authoredContext:
The lab setup shows a string attached to a string vibrator, which oscillates the string with an adjustable frequency f. The other end of the string passes over a frictionless pulley and is tied to a hanging mass. The magnitude of the tension in the string is equal to the weight of the hanging mass. The string has a constant linear density (mass per length) μ and the speed at which a wave travels down the string equals v=FTμ=mgμ another section. The symmetrical boundary conditions (a node at each end) dictate the possible frequencies that can excite standing waves. Starting from a frequency of zero and slowly increasing the frequency, the first mode n=1 appears as shown in the figure. The first mode, also called the fundamental mode or the first harmonic, shows half of a wavelength has formed, so the wavelength is equal to twice the length between the nodes λ1=2L. The fundamental frequency, or first harmonic frequency, that drives this mode is

The standing wave patterns that are possible for a string, the first four of which are shown in the figure, are known as the normal modes, with frequencies known as the normal frequencies. In summary, the first frequency to produce a normal mode is called the fundamental frequency (or first harmonic). Any frequencies above the fundamental frequency are overtones. The second frequency of the n=2 normal mode of the string is the first overtone (or second harmonic). The frequency of the n=3 normal mode is the second overtone (or third harmonic) and so on.

Standing waves created on a string of length L. A node occurs at each end of the string. The nodes are boundary conditions that limit the possible frequencies that excite standing waves. (Note that the amplitudes of the oscillations have been kept constant for visualization. The standing wave patterns possible on the string are known as the normal modes. Conducting this experiment in the lab would result in a decrease in amplitude as the frequency increases.)

It is labeled lambda 2 = L, lambda 2 = 2 by 2 times L. The third figure has three nodes. It is labeled 3 by 2 times lambda 3 = L, lambda 3 = 2 by 3 times L. The fourth figure has 4 nodes. It is labeled 4 by 2 times lambda 4 = L, lambda 4 = 2 by 4 times L. There is a derived formula at the bottom, lambda n equal to 2 by n times L for n = 1, 2, 3 and so on.

plan.concept: A string fixed at both ends can only vibrate in normal modes whose wavelength packs an exact integer number of half-wavelengths into the length L, giving the quantized relation lambda_n = 2L/n.
elements: top reference line between two black endpoint dots, each labeled 'Node'
double-headed dimension arrow above the reference line labeled 'L'
active standing-wave envelope: dark blue curve plus pale mirror-image curve outlining the sweep
left mode label 'n = k' for the selected mode
black endpoint node dots on the active wave (always fixed)
interior node dots on the center line (count = n - 1)
right-side wavelength condition, e.g. 'k/2 * lambda_k = L'
right-side solved wavelength, e.g. 'lambda_k = 2/k * L'
general formula 'lambda_n = (2/n) L,  n = 1, 2, 3, ...' at lower right
horizontal center (equilibrium) line through the wave

interactions.label: Mode number n
interactions.teaches: Stepping n adds one half-wavelength inside the same fixed length L: the envelope gains one more loop and one more interior node, and the right-hand equation updates to n/2 * lambda_n = L, making the integer-fit condition explicit

interactions.label: Oscillate this mode
interactions.teaches: Playing the motion shows the string sweeping between the two envelope curves while the endpoint and interior nodes never move and the antinodes swing through maximum amplitude — clarifying the difference between a node (zero displacement always) and an antinode (maximum displacement)

interactions.label: String length L
interactions.teaches: Dragging the endpoint separation stretches or contracts the whole pattern for the selected mode, and the displayed wavelength lambda_n = 2L/n scales in direct proportion to L, showing that L sets the absolute wavelength while n sets how many half-waves fit

demo_steps.title: Fundamental mode
demo_steps.narration: For n = 1 exactly one half-wavelength fits between the pinned ends, so (1/2) lambda_1 = L and lambda_1 = 2L. The two envelope curves show the full sweep; the ends are the only nodes.

demo_steps.title: Add half-wavelengths
demo_steps.narration: Step to n = 2, then n = 3 and n = 4: each step packs one more half-wavelength into the same L, adding one interior node and one more loop, with the right-hand equation tracking n/2 * lambda_n = L.

demo_steps.title: Nodes vs antinodes
demo_steps.narration: Press play: the string oscillates between the envelope curves. Watch that every node (endpoints and interior crossings) stays perfectly still while the antinodes at the loop peaks swing widest.

demo_steps.title: Length sets the wavelength
demo_steps.narration: Drag the L slider: the pattern and its quoted wavelength lambda_n = 2L/n stretch or shrink together, confirming that the fixed length L, not the mode number alone, fixes the actual wavelength.

plan.keyInsight: Because both ends are pinned nodes, only wavelengths that fit an exact integer number of half-wavelengths into L are allowed, quantizing the standing waves to lambda_n = 2L/n.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Lay out a single active mode panel rather than four stacked rows, since the mode stepper replaces the stack: top shows the reference line with two black 'Node' dots and a double-headed arrow labeled L; below it the active wave drawn as a solid dark-blue sine-half-loop curve with a pale light-blue mirror image forming the envelope, ends pinned at black dots and interior nodes as small dots on a thin horizontal equilibrium line. Left of the wave put 'n = k'; right put the two equations 'k/2 * lambda_k = L' and 'lambda_k = 2/k * L' in italic serif math styling; keep the general 'lambda_n = (2/n) L,  n = 1, 2, 3, ...' pinned at lower right at all times. Use a clear blue for the live curve and a desaturated pale blue for the mirror envelope so the sweep region reads as one shape. When oscillating, animate the live curve's amplitude between the two envelopes while node dots remain fixed. Optionally render the other three modes as faint grey thumbnails down the left margin for orientation, but keep the active mode visually dominant.

discrepancies: Source shows all four harmonic modes (n=1,2,3,4) stacked vertically for direct at-a-glance comparison; the generated figure displays only one mode at a time in the main area, relegating the other three to tiny left-side thumbnails.
The left thumbnails are very small, grey, and carry no wavelength equations, so the source's per-row '(n/2)λn = L' / 'λn = (2/n)L' annotations are absent for the non-active modes.
The hand-built fraction glyphs (numerator/line/denominator) for (n/2) and (2/n) are noticeably more cramped and lower-contrast than the cleanly typeset fractions in the source.
evaluation.notes: The physics, colors, node/L-arrow markers, and per-mode wavelength equations are all correct and the mode/oscillate/length interactions are genuinely functional, but replacing the source's four stacked harmonic rows with a single-mode-plus-thumbnail layout weakens at-a-glance recognizability and hides the wavelength-shrinking progression behind interaction.
action_items: Render all four modes (n=1..4) stacked vertically by default to match the source composition, and use the mode buttons to highlight/enlarge one row rather than hiding the other three.
Attach the '(n/2)λn = L' and 'λn = (2/n)L' equation pair to every visible mode row, not just the active one, so each row is self-explanatory as in the source.
Increase the equation font size and the numerator/denominator spacing so the fractions read comfortably at inline size.
plan_action_items: Revise the layout plan from a single-mode-with-toggle design to a four-row stacked layout (matching the source) where interaction highlights a row, preserving the immediate visual comparison of how wavelength shrinks as n increases.
